questions.q: What is visual hierarchy and how do you create it?
questions.a: The order in which the eye reads a screen. You create it with size, weight, colour, position and spacing, using as few of them as possible per step.

points.title: Follow-up
items: Point at a screen and say what is read first, second and third. Is that the intended order?

questions.q: What is the difference between an affordance and a signifier?
questions.a: An affordance is what an object lets you do; a signifier is the cue that tells you. A flat text label can be tappable (affordance) and give no hint of it (missing signifier).

points.title: Follow-up
items: How do you signal tappability without a button shape?

questions.q: How would you find out why users abandon checkout?
questions.a: Look at funnel analytics for the step with the drop, watch session recordings or run five usability sessions on that step, form a hypothesis, then test a change with an A/B test.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What would you measure besides conversion?

questions.q: What is progressive disclosure?
questions.a: Showing only what is needed now and revealing the rest on demand. A delivery instructions field hidden behind “Add a note” is an example.

questions.q: Why should colour not be the only way to convey state?
questions.a: Colour vision differences, bright sunlight and greyscale modes all remove it. Pair colour with text, an icon or a shape.

points.title: Follow-up
items: Give an example from an order-tracking screen.

questions.q: How does a dark theme differ from an inverted light theme?
questions.a: Dark surfaces use steps of dark grey for elevation, accents get lighter and less saturated, and pure white text is softened. Inversion gets contrast and depth wrong.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How does Material express elevation in dark theme?

questions.q: Line height versus leading versus paragraph spacing?
questions.a: Line height is baseline to baseline. Leading is the extra space added to the font’s natural line. Paragraph spacing is the gap between paragraphs. Figma exposes line height and paragraph spacing.

points.title: Follow-up
items: Why might the same line height look different on iOS and Android?

questions.q: How do you support Dynamic Type with a custom font?
questions.a: Scale the custom size with the system curve: UIFontMetrics in UIKit, a relativeTo text style or ScaledMetric in SwiftUI. Then test at the largest accessibility size.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What do you do when the layout breaks at that size?

questions.q: Why an 8 point grid?
questions.a: It gives a small set of spacing values that scale to whole pixels at 1x, 2x and 3x and produces visible rhythm. A 4 point half-step covers tight cases such as icon padding.

points.title: Follow-up
items: When would you break the grid?

questions.q: What is the difference between responsive and adaptive?
questions.a: Responsive: one layout that stretches and reflows with width. Adaptive: different layouts or components chosen at breakpoints, such as a navigation bar on phones and a rail on tablets.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How do Compose window size classes fit in?

questions.q: Frame versus group?
questions.a: A frame has its own size, constraints, layout grid, Auto Layout and clipping. A group is only a selection wrapper sized by its children. Use frames for anything that maps to a view.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What goes wrong at handoff when a design is all groups?

questions.q: What do constraints do?
questions.a: They decide how a layer moves or stretches when its parent frame resizes: pin left, right, both, centre or scale. Inside Auto Layout, sizing modes replace them, except for absolutely positioned children.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How do constraints map to iOS Auto Layout constraints?

questions.q: Hug, fill and fixed?
questions.a: Hug sizes a frame to its children. Fill makes a child take the remaining space in its parent. Fixed is an explicit number. A parent cannot hug on an axis where a child is filling.

points.title: Follow-up
items: Why can a parent not hug while a child fills?

questions.q: When do you use absolute position inside Auto Layout?
questions.a: For a child that should not take part in the flow, such as a badge on a corner or a close button over an image.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What is the code equivalent on each platform?

questions.q: Variant versus component property?
questions.a: Variants are separate designs grouped as one component set and chosen by property values. Boolean, text and instance-swap properties change one component without multiplying variants.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How many variants does a button with 3 sizes, 4 styles and 5 states need, and how do properties reduce that?

questions.q: How should a Figma component map to code?
questions.a: One component set to one code component; variant properties to enum parameters; boolean and text properties to parameters; instance swap to a slot. Names should match.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What do you do when the Figma API of a component does not match the code API?

questions.q: Variable versus style?
questions.a: A variable holds a single value (colour, number, string, boolean) and can have modes. A style is a saved bundle such as a text style or effect. Styles can reference variables.

points.title: Follow-up
items: Where would you still use a style?

questions.q: Why have a semantic layer?
questions.a: It separates the value from its job, so themes and brands change the mapping without touching components.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How many layers is too many?

questions.q: What belongs in a design system besides components?
questions.a: Foundations (colour, type, spacing, motion), patterns, content guidelines, accessibility rules, documentation, a contribution process and versioning.

points.title: Follow-up
items: Who decides when a one-off becomes a system component?

questions.q: How do you keep Figma and code in sync?
questions.a: A single token source with generated platform files, matching component names and APIs, Code Connect or similar mapping, visual regression tests and a shared changelog.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What breaks first when they drift?

questions.q: When do you use a sheet versus a push?
questions.a: Push for moving deeper in a hierarchy. Sheet for a self-contained task or a brief choice that the user completes or cancels.

points.title: Follow-up
items: When is a full-screen cover right?

questions.q: What is the safe area?
questions.a: The region not covered by bars, the home indicator, the sensor housing or rounded corners. Backgrounds may extend past it; content and controls should not.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How does it change in landscape?

questions.q: What is dynamic colour?
questions.a: On Android 12 and later, Material can derive the app’s colour scheme from the user’s wallpaper. Roles stay the same; values come from the system.

points.title: Follow-up
items: When should a brand opt out?

questions.q: How does Material 3 show elevation?
questions.a: Mainly through tonal surface colours (surface container levels), with shadows used sparingly.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How does that differ from iOS?

questions.q: Material, Cupertino or custom?
questions.a: Material by default; adaptive constructors for controls users notice; a custom system for strong brands. Decide per component, not once for the app.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What does a custom component need to do for accessibility?

questions.q: How do constraints work in Flutter?
questions.a: Constraints go down, sizes go up, the parent sets position. A widget cannot choose a size outside its parent’s constraints.

points.title: Follow-up
items: Why does a ListView inside a Column throw?

questions.q: What does a product card need for a screen reader?
questions.a: One focusable element or a sensible order, a label with name, quantity, price and discount, a button role and label for the action, and no separate stop on decorative images.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How do you test this on each platform?

questions.q: What is reduced motion and how do you honour it?
questions.a: A system setting for people who are affected by motion. Replace large movement with a fade or no animation; keep essential feedback.

points.title: Follow-up
items: Where do you read the setting on iOS, Android and Flutter?

questions.q: What do you check before starting on a new screen?
questions.a: Every state (loading, empty, error, long text), component and token names, spacing as Auto Layout values, assets and export settings, interaction notes, and open questions written as comments.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What do you do when a state is missing?

questions.q: When should an interface animation use ease out, and when ease in?
questions.a: Ease out for things entering or responding to a touch: they start fast, so the interface feels immediate, and settle gently. Ease in for things leaving, which accelerate away. Ease in and out for movement between two on-screen positions.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What would you use for a gesture-driven drag that the user releases mid-way?

questions.q: How do you respect a user’s reduced-motion setting?
questions.a: Read the system setting, keep the feedback, and replace movement, zoom and parallax with a fade or an instant change. Stop looping and auto-playing motion. Never remove the confirmation itself.

points.title: Follow-up
items: Where is the setting read on iOS, Android and Flutter?

questions.q: How do you make one screen work from a small phone to a tablet?
questions.a: Let content set sizes instead of fixing them, define breakpoints by available width and not by device, change structure at those widths (columns, a side pane, a navigation rail), and test with large text and long content at each.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What changes at a breakpoint besides the number of columns?

questions.q: What breaks first when the user doubles their text size?
questions.a: Fixed-height containers clip, single-line rows overflow, and side-by-side layouts run out of width. The fixes are heights that hug content, rows that wrap or stack, and truncation only where the full text is available elsewhere.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How would you test this before release?

questions.q: What is a golden test?
questions.a: A test that renders a widget or screen and compares the image with a stored reference. Flutter calls them golden tests; iOS and Android use snapshot or screenshot tests. They catch unintended visual changes in CI.

points.title: Follow-up
items: Why do goldens flake across machines?
